slides.title: Key questions

paragraphs.text: Key questions
Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service in three Midwest cities, in 2027, and reach profit within its $12.0M cash?
Will Midwest shoppers order often enough, at an acquisition cost we can carry, to fill nine dark stores?
Can a Parcelbird dark store reach contribution profit per order by month 18?
Does the launch fit within $12.0M of cash while keeping 12 months of runway?
Would the same cash do more in the software business?
What should the board decide in January, and what would make us reopen the question?
Decision maker
Success criteria
Timing
Out of scope
The board: two founders and two investors
A path to profitability within the current $12.0M cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; No harm to the growth of the software business
Board meeting, January 2027
A new funding round; Cities beyond the three; Buying an incumbent

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; sell fast delivery to grocers as software instead
Quick commerce is growing, but shoppers are not loyal enough to fill a store affordably
–	US quick-commerce sales grew 42% in 2025, to $5.1B
–	Filling nine stores would take about $27M of paid acquisition
No observed dark store makes money per order; only the founders' plan does
–	At benchmark medians a store loses about $6 on every order
–	Our own pop-up lost about $12.60 an order
The launch breaks the 12-month runway rule even if every plan assumption holds
–	The plan needs $9.5M; only $7.2M sits above the runway floor
Software is the better use of the cash, and its grocers want fast delivery
–	The grocer pipeline is worth 87% of today's ARR, for $0.8M a year of hires
Decline the launch, build fast delivery for grocers, reopen only if four signals turn
–	Grocer software alone meets both investor tests, and goes live in Q3 2027
